title: Atomic Basics: The Safety Inspection
description: Test your knowledge of atoms, isotopes, and natural radiation!

questions.question: What particle in an atom determines which element it is?
questions.explanation: The number of protons (atomic number) determines the element. Carbon always has 6 protons, oxygen has 8, uranium has 92, etc. Change the proton count, and you have a different element!

questions.question: What are isotopes?
options: Atoms with different numbers of protons
Atoms with different numbers of neutrons
Atoms with different numbers of electrons
questions.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same protons) with different numbers of neutrons. For example, Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 are both carbon (6 protons) but have 6 and 8 neutrons respectively.

questions.question: All isotopes are radioactive and dangerous.
questions.explanation: False! Most isotopes are completely stable. You're made mostly of stable isotopes like Carbon-12, Oxygen-16, and Nitrogen-14. Only isotopes with unstable neutron-to-proton ratios are radioactive.

questions.question: An atom has 8 protons, 8 neutrons, and 10 electrons. What is it?
questions.explanation: 8 protons = oxygen (atomic number 8). But it has 10 electrons (2 more than protons), making it negatively charged: O²⁻ ion. Neutral oxygen would have 8 electrons.

questions.question: What percentage of average human radiation exposure comes from natural sources?
questions.explanation: About 80% comes from natural sources: cosmic rays (space), terrestrial radiation (rocks/soil), radon gas, and internal sources (potassium-40 in our bodies). Only ~20% comes from human activities, mostly medical procedures.

questions.question: Which is the LARGEST natural source of radiation exposure for most people?
questions.explanation: Radon gas is the largest single source of natural radiation exposure, contributing about 50% of our natural background dose. It comes from uranium decay in rocks and soil and can accumulate in basements.

questions.question: Living in Denver, Colorado exposes you to more cosmic radiation than living at sea level.
questions.explanation: True! Denver is at high altitude (~1 mile above sea level), so there's less atmosphere to shield cosmic rays from space. People in Denver receive about 2x more cosmic radiation than people at sea level.

questions.question: What makes an isotope unstable (radioactive)?
questions.explanation: An imbalanced neutron-to-proton ratio makes isotopes unstable. Too many or too few neutrons causes the nucleus to decay, emitting radiation to reach a more stable configuration.

questions.question: Where are protons and neutrons located in an atom?
questions.explanation: Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus at the center of the atom. The nucleus is incredibly dense and tiny - if an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be the size of a marble at the center!

questions.question: Carbon-14 is used in carbon dating. Why does it work?
options: C-14 decays at a predictable rate (half-life)
questions.explanation: Carbon-14 is radioactive and decays at a predictable rate (half-life of 5,730 years). Living things constantly replace C-14, but when they die, the C-14 starts decaying. By measuring how much C-14 remains, we can determine how long ago the organism died!

title: Nuclear in Everyday Life
description: See how nuclear tech shows up in health, food, and industry.

questions.question: Which medical use relies on radiation to image inside the body?
questions.explanation: PET scans use positron-emitting tracers to produce detailed images.

questions.question: Food irradiation primarily helps with what?
questions.explanation: Irradiation kills bacteria and pests to improve safety and shelf life.

questions.question: Which industrial use relies on radiation to gauge the thickness of a material?
questions.explanation: Beta/gamma gauges measure material thickness in paper and steel production.

questions.question: Smoke detectors often use a tiny radioactive source to sense smoke.
questions.explanation: Ionization smoke detectors use a minute americium-241 source to detect smoke particles.

questions.question: What is a key environmental benefit of nuclear power?
questions.explanation: Nuclear plants generate electricity with very low operational CO2 emissions.

title: Nuclear Reactions Checkpoint
description: Review fission, fusion, and radioactive decay before wrapping up Unit 2.

questions.question: What is the key difference between fission and fusion?
options: Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei
Fission joins light nuclei; fusion splits heavy nuclei
questions.explanation: Fission splits heavy nuclei like U-235, releasing energy and neutrons. Fusion joins light nuclei like hydrogen isotopes, releasing even more energy per reaction.

questions.question: Why can a power reactor not explode like a nuclear bomb?
options: Reactor fuel is not enriched enough and the design keeps the chain reaction controlled
questions.explanation: Reactor fuel is only a few percent enriched and is moderated and controlled by control rods and coolant. Bombs need very high enrichment and a rapid, uncontrolled supercritical assembly.

questions.question: What do control rods do in a fission reactor?
options: Absorb neutrons to regulate the chain reaction
questions.explanation: Control rods made from materials like boron or cadmium absorb excess neutrons, keeping the reactor at a steady, critical state.

questions.question: Which challenge makes fusion hard to achieve on Earth?
options: Need to overcome the repulsion between positively charged nuclei
questions.explanation: Positively charged nuclei repel each other. Fusion needs extremely high temperatures and/or pressures plus good confinement to push them close enough to fuse.

questions.question: Gamma decay changes an element into a different element.
questions.explanation: Gamma decay only releases energy as photons. It leaves the proton and neutron counts unchanged, so the element stays the same.

questions.question: What does a half-life describe?
options: Time for all radioactive atoms to decay
Time for half of a radioactive sample to decay
Time for radiation to become dangerous
Time for a reactor to reach full power
questions.explanation: Half-life is the predictable time it takes for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.

questions.question: Which reaction powers the Sun?
questions.explanation: The Sun and all stars shine because of hydrogen fusion—mainly the fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium.

title: Radiation Effects Checkpoint
description: Test how radiation interacts with people and matter.

questions.question: Which type of radiation is most penetrating?
questions.explanation: Gamma rays are highly penetrating electromagnetic waves; alpha is the least penetrating.

questions.question: What does half-life describe?
options: Time for all atoms to decay
Time for half of a sample to decay
questions.explanation: Half-life is the predictable time for 50% of a radioactive sample to decay.

questions.question: Which health effect is linked to high acute radiation dose?
questions.explanation: A large, short-term dose can cause acute radiation syndrome; lower doses spread over time generally do not.

questions.question: Radiation from a medical X-ray makes you radioactive afterward.
questions.explanation: Diagnostic X-rays pass through the body; they do not leave you radioactive.

questions.question: Which everyday source contributes the most natural background dose for most people?
questions.explanation: Radon gas from the ground is usually the largest contributor to natural background dose.

title: Radiation Safety Basics
description: Test your knowledge of radiation safety and protection measures

questions.question: Which type of radiation can be stopped by a sheet of paper?
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are the least penetrating form of radiation and can be stopped by a sheet of paper or even the outer layer of skin.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of control rods in a nuclear reactor?
options: To absorb neutrons and control the reaction rate
questions.explanation: Control rods are made of neutron-absorbing materials like boron or cadmium. They regulate the nuclear chain reaction by absorbing neutrons.

questions.question: Nuclear power plants can explode like nuclear bombs.
questions.explanation: False. Nuclear power plants cannot explode like nuclear bombs. The fuel is not enriched enough, and the physics of the reactor design prevents such an explosion.

questions.question: What is the half-life of a radioactive substance?
options: The time it takes to become completely safe
The time it takes for half of the atoms to decay
The time it takes to reach maximum radiation
The time it takes to double in size
questions.explanation: Half-life is the time required for half of the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay. After each half-life, the radioactivity is reduced by 50%.

questions.question: Which material is most commonly used for gamma radiation shielding?
questions.explanation: Lead is the most common material for gamma radiation shielding due to its high density and atomic number, which effectively absorbs gamma rays.

questions.question: What does ALARA stand for in radiation safety?
options: Automatic Level Adjustment for Radiation Activity
Advanced Laboratory for Atomic Research Applications
questions.explanation: ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) is a radiation safety principle that aims to minimize radiation exposure to the lowest practical level.

title: Radiation Types & Shielding
description: Identify alpha, beta, and gamma characteristics and how to shield them.

questions.question: Which barrier is enough to stop alpha particles?
questions.explanation: A sheet of paper or skin stops alpha particles; they are not very penetrating.

questions.question: Which material is best for shielding beta particles?
questions.explanation: Low-density materials like aluminum or plastic effectively stop beta particles.

questions.question: Which is pure electromagnetic radiation?
questions.explanation: Gamma rays are high-energy photons, unlike particle radiation.

questions.question: Gamma shielding often uses dense materials like lead or concrete.
questions.explanation: Dense materials provide better attenuation for penetrating gamma rays.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about exposure risk?
options: Alpha is harmless in any situation
Beta is always more dangerous than gamma
Alpha is dangerous if inhaled/ingested despite weak penetration
questions.explanation: Alpha cannot penetrate skin but is hazardous if inside the body.

title: Reactor Mechanics Check
description: Confirm how reactors control fission and produce power.

questions.question: What do control rods primarily do?
options: Absorb neutrons to regulate the chain reaction
questions.explanation: Control rods absorb excess neutrons, keeping the reactor critical but controlled.

questions.question: Why is coolant flow important?
options: It removes heat and transfers it to make steam
questions.explanation: Coolant carries heat from the core to steam generators or turbines for electricity.

questions.question: Which design feature slows down neutrons in many reactors?
questions.explanation: Moderators slow neutrons to sustain a thermal fission chain reaction.

questions.question: Commercial power reactors use weapons-grade highly enriched uranium.
questions.explanation: Power reactors use low-enriched fuel (around 3–5% U-235), far below weapons levels.

questions.question: What starts the turbines to generate electricity?
questions.explanation: Heat from fission boils water to steam, which spins turbines connected to generators.

title: Nuclear Safety & Security
description: Check your understanding of reactor safety systems and safeguards.

questions.question: What is the role of containment buildings?
options: Provide a barrier to keep radioactivity inside
questions.explanation: Containment is a reinforced barrier to prevent radioactive releases.

questions.question: Which international agency sets safety standards and shares best practices?
questions.explanation: The IAEA develops safety standards and coordinates peer reviews among member states.

questions.question: What do physical protection systems guard against?
options: Theft or sabotage of nuclear material and facilities
questions.explanation: Security systems deter and detect theft or sabotage of nuclear material and assets.

questions.question: Defense-in-depth means relying on a single safety barrier.
questions.explanation: Defense-in-depth uses multiple redundant and diverse safety layers, not just one.

questions.question: What is the main aim of nuclear safeguards?
options: Verify nuclear material is not diverted to weapons
questions.explanation: IAEA safeguards include inspections and accounting to ensure peaceful use of nuclear material.

title: Sustainability & Waste
description: Gauge your grasp of nuclear energy’s environmental footprint and waste.

questions.question: Compared to coal, nuclear power emits how much CO₂ during operation?
questions.explanation: Nuclear plants have very low operational CO₂ emissions compared to fossil plants.

questions.question: What is the typical strategy for managing used nuclear fuel initially?
options: On-site pool cooling then dry cask storage
questions.explanation: Fuel is cooled in spent fuel pools, then often moved to robust dry cask storage.

questions.question: Why is high energy density of nuclear fuel an environmental benefit?
options: It means far less fuel volume and mining per kWh
questions.explanation: High energy density means small fuel amounts produce large energy, reducing mining and material throughput.

questions.question: Long-lived nuclear waste cannot be contained safely.
questions.explanation: Engineered barriers, dry casks, and deep geological repositories are designed to safely isolate long-lived waste.

questions.question: Which description best fits the role nuclear power plays in a clean electricity grid?
questions.explanation: Nuclear provides firm, dispatchable low-carbon power that complements variable renewables.
